papers.what_it_is: Theory-plus-numerics preprint proving exponential memory separations between a polylog-size quantum computer using quantum oracle sketching and memory-limited classical machines.
papers.title_on_page_1: Exponential quantum advantage in processing massive classical data

assertions.value: Theorem 3 (main text, informal statement; formalized as Theorem F.11): using O~(N) samples, a quantum computer of poly(log D) size solves the binary classification task with N items and D-dimensional features, while any classical machine of O(D^0.99) size cannot.
quotes: Using O˜(N ) samples, a quantum computer with poly(log D) size can solve the binary classification task with N items and D-dimensional features, whereas any classical machine with O(D0.99) size cannot.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a theorem by the authors with a formal version in the appendix; proof not independently checked here.

assertions.value: Formal Theorem F.11: with O~(RN) samples a quantum machine of poly(log D) size solves the classification task with high success probability, while any classical machine of o(D^(1-zeta)) size, for any constant zeta > 0, cannot succeed with probability above 1/2 + 1/N^omega(1).
quotes: Using O˜(RN ) samples, a quantum machine with poly(log D) size can solve it with high success probability, while any classical machine with o(D1−ζ) size for any constant ζ > 0 cannot
assertions.certainty_reason: Formal theorem statement; the proof was located but not read line by line.

assertions.value: The Discussion states that the runtime of quantum oracle sketching is dominated by the O~(N) data loading time, and that this loading time is unavoidable only under the condition that each gate has a constant number of degrees of freedom.
quotes: The runtime of quantum oracle sketching is dominated by the O˜(N ) data loading time, which is unavoidable if each gate has only a constant number of degrees of freedom,
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state it plainly, but as a conditional remark, not a theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state their exponential space separation reaches the ultimate limit allowed by quantum mechanics, because a classical machine of O~(N) size can always store the full dataset.
quotes: our exponential separation reaches the ultimate limit allowed by quantum mechanics, since a classical machine with O˜(N ) size can always store the full dataset
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' interpretive claim backed by a short argument and citations; the implied need for a memory-restricted classical machine is a consequence, not stated in these words.

assertions.value: In numerical experiments on real-world datasets the authors report quantum advantages of four to six orders of magnitude in memory using fewer than 60 logical qubits.
quotes: This yields quantum advantages of four to six orders of magnitude using fewer than 60 logical qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical comparison of memory counts, not a hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors extrapolate the scaling to hundreds of logical qubits outperforming extremely large classical systems, and state the extrapolation ignores the exponential runtime overhead.
quotes: Extrapolating this scaling, while ignoring the exponential runtime overhead, suggests that relatively small quantum devices with hundreds of logical qubits could outperform even extremely large classical systems, barring unforeseen limitations to quantum mechanics.
assertions.certainty_reason: Explicitly labeled extrapolation with a stated caveat.

facts.explanation: Theorem 3 is stated correctly, but the fact omits the O~(N) sample count and uses the informal D^0.99 form (formal Theorem F.11 uses o(D^(1-zeta))). The Discussion says data loading time dominates runtime, but calls it unavoidable only IF each gate has a constant number of degrees of freedom. Dropping that condition overstates it.

The Discussion says the separation reaches the ultimate limit allowed by quantum mechanics because an O~(N) classical machine can store the dataset. That the separation needs a memory-restricted classical machine follows directly but is not worded so in the paper. 'Ultimate limit' is the authors' claim.

Part 1: fewer than 60 logical qubits and the extrapolation caveat (ignoring exponential runtime overhead) are both in the paper; the extrapolation says hundreds of qubits. Part 2: no universe, atom, or 300 text found in the extraction. Part 3 is supported by the blog record. Scope note: the absence rests on text extraction only.

assertions.value: Markidis reports that the compiled circuits of the offline QOS realization remain too deep for current quantum computing devices.
quotes: However, the compiled circuits remain too deep for current quantum computing devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: Abstract statement backed by transpiled depth measurements in the body.

assertions.value: After exact phase fusion the offline circuits still need depths of several hundred thousand gates and the author calls them impractical on current devices; measured on the DNA fingerprinting case study.
quotes: The fused implementations, studied here, still require depths of several hundred thousand gates and remain impractical on current quantum computing devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: Transpiled resource counts for one task and one implementation.

assertions.value: The offline realization does not retain the machine size advantage proved for online QOS and results in deep quantum circuits.
quotes: However, it does not retain the machine size advantage proved for online QOS and results in deep quantum circuits.

assertions.value: Markidis concludes QOS remains a forward-looking data access model, not a method that can be effectively deployed on current quantum computing devices.
quotes: QOS remains a forward-looking data access model rather than a method that can be effectively deployed on current quantum computing devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author conclusion from one case study.

facts.explanation: Supported: compiled circuits remain too deep for current devices, from one DNA fingerprinting case study. Overstated if read broadly: the circuits are the author's OFFLINE realization, which the paper says does not retain the online QOS machine-size advantage. The study uses synthetic data (N=32 sequences). Independence is inferred from a different author and institution; authorship of the original QOS work was not checked beyond affiliations.
